before: An array keeps values in order and can contain duplicates. A Set keeps each distinct value once.

```swift
let colors = Set(["blue", "green", "blue"])
print(colors.count)
```
The count is 2 because blue appears only once in the set.
Use contains to ask whether a set includes a value. Inserting a value already present does not increase the count.

```swift
var colors: Set<String> = ["blue"]
colors.insert("blue")
colors.insert("red")
print(colors.contains("red"))
print(colors.count)
```
The results are true and 2.
A set does not promise an iteration order. Call sorted() when the displayed output needs a predictable order; this returns an array.

```swift
let tags = ["music", "art", "music"]
let unique = Set(tags)
print(unique.sorted())
```
The array is ["art", "music"]. The original tags array is unchanged.
For the exercise, return the unique activity names in ascending order. Keep exact spelling: "Read" and "read" are different strings. Empty input returns an empty array.
after: A Set keeps each distinct value once. An array can contain repeats, so turning an array into a Set removes duplicate values from the new collection.
A Set does not promise the order in which you will visit its values. `sorted()` returns an array in order when you need predictable output.

```swift
let tags = ["music", "art", "music"]
let unique = Set(tags)
print(unique.sorted())
```
The result is `["art", "music"]`. The two matching music entries become one, then sorting puts art first.
`Set(tags)` creates a set value from the array. It does not remove items from the original `tags` array.
Exact matching matters. `Read` and `read` differ, so both remain. This task does not change letter case or use language-specific sorting rules.
An empty input becomes an empty Set. Sorting it returns an empty array. There is no special placeholder item to add.
